106.title: Shabbat afternoon
106.hook: rest, a nap, a walk, study and friends; the Talmud calls Shabbat one sixtieth of the world to come (Berakhot 57b)
106.howItsDone: Shabbat afternoon is often spent after a long lunch napping, walking, visiting friends, playing with children and studying; some communities read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on summer Shabbat afternoons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, melacha: thirty-nine kinds of creative work, set aside. Your line was not doing is a practice. What did you skip, and what filled the space? Day one hundred six.

Saturday, about two in the afternoon. Lunch was long. The dishes can wait. Somebody's asleep on the couch with a book open on their chest. The kids are out in the yard, or at a friend's house down the street. Two neighbors are walking slowly, not going anywhere in particular. Someone's reading. There's nowhere to drive to, nothing to buy, no screen to check. If you've never had an afternoon like this, it can sound boring. Some who have one every week say it's the part of the week they'd give up last. Today: menuchah, rest.
screen: `SATURDAY, TWO IN THE AFTERNOON.` → `A BOOK OPEN ON SOMEONE'S CHEST.` → `NOWHERE TO GO.`

segments.voice: Menuchah means rest, but a full, settled kind of rest, not just collapse. There's a well-known teaching about Genesis. It says God finished the work on the seventh day, and the rabbis asked: what was still missing, that was finished on the seventh day? And they answered: rest. The world had everything, except menuchah. Came Shabbat, came rest. Rest isn't the absence of creation. It's the last thing created. The prophet Isaiah gave Shabbat a name people still use, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "call the sabbath a delight." Oneg, delight. So Shabbat afternoon is for delight. A nap, which some people half joke is a religious duty. A slow walk. Friends dropping by. Games with the kids. And study. In some communities, on summer Shabbat afternoons, people read Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a chapter a week. Then there's the Talmud's line about this. In a list of things that are one sixtieth of something greater, it says: fire is one sixtieth of Gehinnom, the place of punishment, honey is one sixtieth of manna, sleep is one sixtieth of death, a dream is one sixtieth of prophecy, and Shabbat is one sixtieth of the world to come. A small taste of it. A sample. The rabbis weren't describing the afternoon as a holiday from life. They were describing it as a preview of what life is ultimately for. Whatever you believe about what's coming, the afternoon itself asks something simple. Stop long enough to taste something, and see if it's good.
screen: `MENUCHAH: SETTLED REST.` · `THE WORLD LACKED ONLY REST.` · `CALL THE SABBATH A DELIGHT.` · `ONE SIXTIETH OF THE WORLD TO COME.` · then, large: `A TASTE OF WHAT'S COMING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a real nap or a slow walk. Not right now, but let's plan it. Settle, and breathe. Feel how heavy your body is in the chair. Let your shoulders drop a little lower. Now picture a stretch of time this week with nothing in it, and choose: a nap, eyes closed, phone in another room, or a walk with no destination and no podcast. Picture yourself doing it slowly. Let yourself look forward to it. The bell holds the time.
Menuchah. Settled rest, the last thing created, and on Shabbat afternoon a taste, the Talmud says, of the world to come.
Your line: a taste of what's coming. Today, take your nap or your walk, and treat it as something good, not something wasted. Day one hundred six.

107.title: The third meal
107.hook: a slow meal at dusk, with quiet songs as the day fades
107.howItsDone: Late on Saturday afternoon, Jews who keep the custom eat a small third meal, at home or in synagogue between the afternoon and evening prayers, often in dim light with slow songs such as Yedid Nefesh and Psalm 23.

segments.voice: Yesterday, menuchah, Shabbat afternoon: a nap, a walk, one sixtieth of the world to come. Your line was a taste of what's coming. Did you take the nap? Day one hundred seven.

The last hour of a good vacation. The bags are packed. The light is going gold. Part of you is already back at work, answering email in your head. And part of you wants to hold on to every last minute. Late on Saturday afternoon, as the sun goes down, Shabbat reaches that hour. And instead of rushing to the end, the custom is to sit down to eat. Again. A small meal, in fading light, with songs that get slower and quieter as the room gets darker. Today: seudah shlishit, the third meal.
screen: `THE LAST HOUR OF A VACATION.` → `THE LIGHT GOES GOLD.` → `SIT DOWN TO EAT, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Seudah means meal and shlishit means third. Friday night dinner is the first Shabbat meal, Saturday lunch is the second, and this is the third. Where does a third meal come from? Back to the manna. When Moses told the people about the first Shabbat, he said, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Eat that to-day; for to-day is a sabbath unto the LORD; to-day ye shall not find it in the field." The rabbis counted: today, today, today. Three times. So, three meals. The third doesn't have to be big. Some people have challah and a little fish or salad. In some communities it happens in the synagogue between the afternoon and evening prayers, at long tables, with the lights low or off. And it's the songs people remember. Slow, longing songs. Some sing the Twenty-third Psalm, the LORD is my shepherd. Others sing Yedid Nefesh, beloved of the soul, a love poem to God by Eleazar Azikri, a Kabbalist of Safed. Hasidic tradition calls this hour a time of special closeness, the favor of favors, when the day's holiness is at its fullest just before it leaves. There's often no talking between the songs. People hum. Someone starts a tune, and it goes around the table again and again. The whole meal is a way of saying: we know it's ending, and we're not going to hurry it along. You stay at the table until you really can't see.
screen: `SEUDAH SHLISHIT: THE THIRD MEAL.` · `TODAY, TODAY, TODAY.` · `SLOW SONGS IN FADING LIGHT.` · `THE FAVOR OF FAVORS.` · then, large: `DON'T HURRY IT ALONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal slowly at dusk. Plan it now. Settle, and breathe. Picture this evening, as the light starts to fade. Picture something simple on a plate. Picture yourself sitting down with no screen, maybe with someone, maybe alone. The first bite, slowly. Notice the light changing on the wall. Hum something, if you like. When the food's gone, stay a minute more, until it's really dark. The bell holds the time.
Seudah shlishit. The third meal: a small, slow meal at dusk on Shabbat, with quiet songs as the day fades.
Your line: don't rush the ending. Today, when something good is ending, a visit, a call, a day off, stay with it for one minute longer than you usually would. Day one hundred seven.

108.title: Havdalah
108.hook: a braided candle, sweet spices and wine separate holy time from the week
108.howItsDone: On Saturday night after three stars appear, Jews say Havdalah over a cup of wine, fragrant spices and a braided candle, then extinguish the candle in the wine and wish each other shavua tov.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seudah shlishit, the third meal, slow songs at dusk. Your line was don't rush the ending. Now the ending comes. Day one hundred eight.

Saturday night. Someone goes to the window, looks up, and counts: one star, two, three. Shabbat is over. But nobody grabs their phone yet. The lights stay low. Someone lights a tall candle with several wicks braided together, and it burns with a big, bright flame, like a small torch. A child holds it up high. There's a cup of wine, filled so full it spills over. And a little box of cloves or cinnamon gets passed from hand to hand, and everybody breathes in. Today: Havdalah.
screen: `ONE STAR, TWO, THREE.` → `A BRAIDED CANDLE, HELD HIGH.` → `A BOX OF SPICES, PASSED AROUND.`

segments.voice: Havdalah means separation, distinction. Shabbat began with Kiddush over a cup, making the time holy. It ends with Havdalah over a cup, marking where holy time stops and the ordinary week starts. Four blessings. One over the wine. One over the spices. One over the fire. And one that praises God for separating, and it names a list of separations, among them holy and ordinary, light and darkness, and the seventh day and the six days of work. Why spices? There's a teaching in the Talmud that on Shabbat a person receives an extra soul, a neshamah yeteirah, a bigger capacity for rest and joy. When Shabbat leaves, the extra soul leaves too, and later teachers say the spices are there to revive you, a little sweetness for the loss. Why fire? Because fire can't be kindled on Shabbat, so the first thing you do when it ends is make light. And there's a story in the midrash that Adam, on the first Saturday night of the world, afraid of the dark, was given the wisdom to strike two stones together and make the first fire. The candle has several wicks because the blessing speaks of the lights of fire, plural. People hold their hands up to the flame and look at the light on their fingernails, using the fire for something before blessing it. Then the candle is put out in the spilled wine, with a hiss. Often a song follows for Elijah the prophet, who tradition says will one day bring the final redemption, and everyone wishes each other shavua tov, a good week. The week begins, but you walk into it smelling of cloves.
screen: `HAVDALAH: SEPARATION.` · `WINE, SPICES, FIRE, DISTINCTION.` · `THE EXTRA SOUL LEAVES.` · `LIGHT ON YOUR FINGERNAILS.` · then, large: `SHAVUA TOV. A GOOD WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smell something fragrant as the week begins. If you have something near you, a spice jar, a lemon, coffee, a flower, soap, pick it up. If not, remember a scent you love. Settle, and breathe. Bring it close, and breathe it in slowly. Let it fill you. Think about what you want to carry from your rest into your busy days: some patience, some quiet, some sweetness. Breathe in once more, as if storing it. The bell holds the time.
Havdalah. Separation: wine, spices and a braided flame on Saturday night, marking where holy time ends and the week begins.
Your line: carry the scent in. Today, as you start something busy, pause and smell something good first. Tomorrow a new part begins: blessings through the day. Day one hundred eight.

109.title: Modeh Ani
109.hook: the first words on waking thank God for returning the soul
109.howItsDone: Many Jews say Modeh Ani immediately on waking, still in bed, before washing their hands or saying any other prayer; children often learn it with a simple tune.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Havdalah: wine, spices and a braided flame to close Shabbat. Your line was carry the scent in. Now the week begins, and so does a new part of the path: blessings through the day. Day one hundred nine.

What's the first thing you do when you wake up? Be honest. For a lot of us, the hand is on the phone before the eyes are fully open. Headlines, messages, the weather, somebody's vacation photos. The first thing that gets into your head decides a lot about the next hour. In Jewish tradition, there's something that's meant to come first, before your feet touch the floor, before you wash, before you check anything. It's twelve Hebrew words long, and children learn it when they're tiny. Today: Modeh Ani.
screen: `THE HAND FINDS THE PHONE.` → `THE FIRST THING IN YOUR HEAD.` → `TWELVE WORDS, BEFORE THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Modeh ani means I thank, or I acknowledge. A woman says modah ani. The whole line, in a plain English rendering, goes like this: I thank you, living and everlasting King, for you have returned my soul to me with compassion; great is your faithfulness. Let's open it up. Returned my soul. There's an old Jewish idea that sleep is a little like death, and that each night the soul is entrusted to God, the way you'd leave a coat at a coat check. In the morning you get it back. And the thanks isn't only for being alive. It's for getting it back with compassion, when maybe you didn't feel you'd earned another day. The last words, great is your faithfulness, come from the book of Lamentations, a book of grief. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the verse says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness." A line written in the ruins, about new mornings. Here's a detail people love. Modeh Ani doesn't use any of the names of God. That's on purpose: it can be said before you've washed your hands, lying in bed, half asleep, even in the dark. You don't have to be ready to say it. And it's young, as prayers go. It first appears in a book from the sixteenth or seventeenth century, though the idea behind it is much older. Many parents say it with small children every morning, sometimes with a little tune. It's a whole philosophy in twelve words: before you want anything from the day, notice that you got the day.
screen: `I THANK YOU.` · `MY SOUL, RETURNED WITH COMPASSION.` · `NEW EVERY MORNING.` · `NO NAME OF GOD, SO SAY IT IN BED.` · then, large: `GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say thank you before you get up. Let's rehearse tomorrow morning now. Settle, and breathe. Imagine you've just woken up. Your eyes are opening. The phone is there, but not yet. Feel the bed under you. Notice you're breathing, that you're here again. If you pray, you can say the twelve words, or just modeh ani. If you don't, say a simple thank you, to whoever or whatever you like, for the day you got. Then, and only then, picture your feet touching the floor. The bell holds the time.
Modeh Ani. I thank you: the first words on waking, thanking God for returning the soul with compassion.
Your line: thank you, first. Tomorrow morning, before your hand finds your phone, say thank you. Put a note by the bed if it helps. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: Washing the hands
110.hook: a cup of water poured over each hand begins the day clean
110.howItsDone: On waking, observant Jews pour water from a two-handled cup over each hand in turn, often three times, and say the blessing al netilat yadayim; the same washing is done before eating bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modeh Ani, twelve words of thanks before your feet touch the floor. Your line was thank you, first. Did you say it this morning? Day one hundred ten.

In some Jewish homes, if you look beside the bed, you'll find a strange little setup: a cup, often with two handles, and a bowl. Sometimes it's plastic, sometimes it's silver, sometimes it's a mug and a salad bowl because that's what was around. It's there so the first thing you do after the thank you is pour water over your hands, right there, before you walk anywhere. It's not about soap. Your hands might already be clean. Today: netilat yadayim, the washing of the hands.
screen: `A CUP AND A BOWL BY THE BED.` → `WATER BEFORE YOU WALK.` → `NOT ABOUT SOAP.`

segments.voice: Netilat yadayim is usually translated as the lifting, or taking, of the hands. Some teachers read that as a picture: after washing, the hands are raised, as if lifting them into the day. Here's how it's usually done in the morning. Fill the cup. The usual custom is right hand first, then left, back and forth, often three times each hand. Then dry them, and say a short blessing that thanks God for the commandment of washing the hands. Why? The rabbis give a few reasons. One is that the priests in the Temple washed their hands and feet before they served, and some teachers compare each morning to a priest beginning a day of holy work. Another is about sleep. We said yesterday that sleep is a little like death, and there's a teaching that some kind of impurity, a heaviness, stays on the hands overnight, and washing lifts it. And the simplest reason: you're starting again. Yesterday's hands did yesterday's things. These hands haven't done anything yet. There's another hand washing, before eating bread, with the same cup and the same blessing. The Talmud ties it to the purity rules for the priests' food, and later teachers add that the table is like an altar. And the two handles? The usual explanation: so the clean hand never touches where the unwashed one held it. It's a small, practical design for a big idea. Every morning, and before every meal with bread, you get a fresh start, poured out of a cup.
screen: `LIFTING OF THE HANDS.` · `RIGHT, LEFT, THREE TIMES.` · `LIKE PRIESTS BEFORE THEY SERVE.` · `BEFORE BREAD, TOO.` · then, large: `THESE HANDS HAVEN'T DONE ANYTHING YET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour water over your hands slowly. If you're near a sink, go to it now, or do this the next time you are. Use a cup if you have one, or just let the water run. Pour over one hand, then the other. Slowly. Feel the water, its temperature, how it runs off your fingers. As it runs, let yesterday go with it: the argument, the mistake, the tired feeling. Dry your hands and look at them: they haven't done anything yet today. The bell holds the time.
Netilat yadayim. The lifting of the hands: water poured from a cup over each hand, on waking and before bread, to begin clean.
Your line: begin clean. Today, each time you wash your hands, slow down for one pour and let something go with the water. Day one hundred ten.

111.title: Asher Yatzar
111.hook: a blessing after the bathroom thanks God for a body whose openings work
111.howItsDone: After using the bathroom and washing their hands, observant Jews say Asher Yatzar; it is also part of the morning blessings, and some homes hang the text near the bathroom door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, netilat yadayim, water poured over each hand. Your line was begin clean. What did you let go with the water? Day one hundred eleven.

The bathroom is not where people go looking for holiness. In, out, wash the hands, back to the day. Unless, of course, something goes wrong. Ask anyone who's had kidney stones, or a bowel obstruction, or a newborn in intensive care who can't yet feed and digest on their own. Then you learn fast how much has to go right, every hour, without you asking. Jewish tradition has a blessing for exactly this. It's said after using the bathroom. Today: Asher Yatzar.
screen: `NOT WHERE YOU'D LOOK FOR HOLY.` → `UNLESS SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `A BLESSING FOR THE BATHROOM.`

segments.voice: Asher yatzar means who formed. The blessing comes from the Talmud, and it's said after you've washed your hands. It praises God, who formed the human being with wisdom, and created in us openings and openings, hollows and hollows. Then it says something startlingly frank: it's known before your throne of glory that if one of them were opened, or one of them were blocked, it would be impossible to survive and stand before you even for a short while. And it ends by blessing God, who heals all flesh and acts wondrously. Openings and hollows. Pipes, valves, tubes, chambers. The rabbis looked at the plumbing of the human body and called it wisdom. Some doctors have written about how differently it reads after you've cared for patients whose bodies stopped doing these ordinary things. The Psalms say something similar, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I will give thanks unto Thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." What makes Asher Yatzar unusual is where it puts the wonder. Not in a sunset or a mountain. In one of the plainest things a body does, several times a day. Jewish tradition doesn't split the body off from the holy. You don't have to be at your most spiritual to bless. You just have to notice that it worked, again. For people living with illness, the blessing can be harder, or it can become a daily thanks for whatever still works. Either way, it's honest about how fragile a body is.
screen: `ASHER YATZAR: WHO FORMED.` · `OPENINGS AND HOLLOWS.` · `IF ONE WERE BLOCKED.` · `WONDER IN THE UNGLAMOROUS.` · then, large: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say thanks once after the bathroom. Practice the noticing now. Settle, and breathe. Feel your breath go in and out, without your help. Feel your heart, if you can. Think of what's happening inside you right now: digesting, filtering, pumping, healing a scratch you forgot about. If something in your body doesn't work well, you can hold that honestly too. Then pick a moment later today, after the bathroom, after washing your hands, to say thank you for what did work. The bell holds the time.
Asher Yatzar. Who formed: the blessing after the bathroom for a body of openings and hollows that work, and for the one who heals all flesh.
Your line: the body is a wonder. Today, once, after the bathroom, pause for three seconds and be glad it all worked. Day one hundred eleven.

112.title: Blessed are you
112.hook: almost every blessing begins "blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe"
112.howItsDone: Blessings over food, commandments and moments open with the six-word formula baruch atah Adonai eloheinu melech ha'olam, followed by words naming the food, act or moment being blessed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asher Yatzar, thanks for a body that works. Your line was the body is a wonder. It's the end of a week: Shabbat afternoon, the third meal, Havdalah, Modeh Ani, washing the hands, and now the words inside every blessing. Day one hundred twelve.

Some phrases get said so often nobody hears them anymore. How are you. Bless you, after a sneeze. Love you, at the end of a call. They're tiny, and they hold a relationship together. In Jewish life there's a phrase like that, said again and again through the day, over bread, over a new fruit, after the bathroom, before lighting candles, on seeing lightning. You've heard pieces of it already on this path. It's six Hebrew words, and the blessings over food, acts and moments start with them. Today: baruch, blessed.
screen: `WORDS YOU DON'T HEAR ANYMORE.` → `SAID AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `SIX WORDS AT THE START.`

segments.voice: Here they are, slowly. Baruch, blessed. Atah, are you. Adonai, Lord. Eloheinu, our God. Melech, king. Ha'olam, of the universe, or of the world. Blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe. Then comes whatever this blessing is for: who brings forth bread, who creates the fruit of the vine. The Talmud says a blessing needs two things to count: God's name, and God's kingship. So the six words carry both. A few things are hiding inside. First, Adonai. It's what's said in place of God's four-letter name, which by long tradition isn't pronounced. Outside of prayer, Jews often avoid even Adonai and say Hashem, the Name, instead. Second, notice the grammar. It begins with you, atah, close and personal, like talking to someone across a table. Then it moves to king of the universe, vast and far. And the next words often shift to who, as if stepping back. Commentators noticed this and said it's on purpose: God is both near enough to speak to and too great to hold. Third, the puzzle. How can a person bless God? God is the source of blessing. Some teachers answer that baruch here means acknowledging God as that source: you are where blessing comes from. Some connect the word bracha with berech, the knee, the way you bow, and with breichah, a pool of water, blessing as something that flows. The Psalms say, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Bless the LORD, O my soul." Six words, and before bread or lightning or anything else, the one saying them has turned toward what they call the source.
